caption:
Most teams buy an observability tool and call it an architecture. 

The interesting part of this diagram isn't the vendor at the end, it's everything before it: a durable buffer so producers and consumers can fail independently, and PII redaction as its own service rather than a policy someone is supposed to follow. 

Compliance built into the pipeline is the difference between an AI system that runs in production and a demo legal shuts down. None of the hard parts here are AI parts.
transcript: This is how booking.com scales AI observability with Arise to those that are interested in enterprise architectures and responsible for figuring out what is a scalable architecture to meet our AI adoption and AI native development needs going forward as a technology team. I found this to be a very interesting use case. This is a really interesting diagram to kind of ground on in terms of their architecture. So on the left you have N number of gen AI applications. They're using an AI telemetry collector. They pull that in, they normalize it, and then they have traces going into a secure message bus. In this case, it looks like they are using a managed Kafka service, so that's a durable buffer that absorbs spikes and decouples producers from consumers, and then they have a PII redaction service. I thought this was really interesting for anybody in enterprise software that has to deal with compliance and regulation and privacy and things like that. So they specifically call that out in their architecture that they have a service that detects and masks PII and span attributes and text fields. And then they go and export to Arise and a warehouse. Redacted traces are sent to Arise in real time and stored in the warehouse for analytics. Arise will then enrich with space, project metadata, etc. And then on the warehouse ingestion side, it looks like these persist to use for offline analytics, long term trends and backfills. And here's another diagram for their ML prediction log pipeline for booking.com from their data warehouse all the way to Arise and then getting to specific data sets that they could use for gen AI applications such as ranking or fraud detection or any other model that they could then fine tune for domain specific problems. One of the biggest takeaways from reading this to me was everybody that is deploying AI architectures at scale. You really need to be thinking about chunking out their services so that you could do this at scale.

creator: techvrix
caption:
This is how AI actually learns. 🧠📉

Backpropagation can be understood by imagining a neural network’s total error as a point on a huge, high-dimensional loss surface, where every direction represents a different model parameter.

Each parameter influences the model’s overall loss, and the gradient combines all of those partial derivatives to show how the loss changes with respect to every parameter.

Using the chain rule, backpropagation efficiently calculates this gradient across the entire network.

The negative gradient points in the direction of steepest descent. You can think of it like rolling a ball downhill, where each step moves the model toward a region with lower loss.

The network repeats this process over and over, adjusting its parameters to gradually reduce error and improve its predictions.

That simple idea, calculate the gradient, move downhill, and repeat, is one of the fundamental mechanisms behind how modern neural networks learn.

Credit: Welch Labs

Follow for more @techvrix

#AI #MachineLearning #DeepLearning #Backpropagation #NeuralNetworks
transcript: We can do this efficiently by computing the slope of each of our parameters with respect to our loss, combining these slopes into a vector called the gradient, and using the gradient to make iterative updates to our weights. Let's explore, as we did last time, how our loss varies with a single model parameter by plotting our loss as a function of m2. Our m2 parameter in our Paris neuron currently has a value of 0, resulting in a loss of 2.45. If we increase the parameter's value to 0.1, we can recompute our outputs, and see that this increases our probability of being in Paris, according to the model, to 0.107, reducing our loss to 2.24. Now, with these two computations of our loss for different values of m2, we've effectively estimated the value of our slope, delta L over delta m2. This tells us that if we increase m2, our loss will go down, increasing model performance. We could theoretically do this for all six parameters in our model, and use these estimated slopes to guide the gradient descent learning process.

caption:
A person’s cancer could become the blueprint for its own treatment!

“Scientists can sequence a tumor, find mutations unique to that cancer, and manufacture a personalized mRNA treatment around them.

Cancer vaccines aren’t new. Personalized MRNA cancer vaccines aren’t even new.

What IS new: Moderna and Merck just reported the first positive Phase 3 result for an individualized neoantigen therapy and an mRNA-based cancer treatment.

1,137 patients. A treatment designed from each individual tumor. And a major test of whether truly personalized medicine can move into the mainstream.

#cancerresearch #mrna #healthtech #biotech #gigaqian
transcript: Okay, Moderna and Merck have just announced that a cancer treatment made using the genetic information inside an individual's tumor has just succeeded in phase three. The medicine they make for one person and the medicine they make for another would literally contain different genetic instructions. They have to sequence a tumor before they can manufacture it. And before someone says, haven't cancer vaccines existed for years? Yes, Russia even reported treating its first patient with a personalized melanoma vaccine this past April. So what actually happened this week? Let me tell you. I'm Giga Chen and in the next 90 seconds, you're going to understand exactly how this works, what a neoantigen is, and why phase three changes the story. First, this isn't a vaccine you take to prevent cancer. These patients already had high-risk melanoma and the surgeons have removed it. Scientists take the tumor and sequence its DNA. DNA is written using four chemical letters A, C, G, and T. Sequencing basically means reading those letters in order. Then you compare the tumor with normal cells from the same person to find the mutations that appeared in the cancer. And this is where it gets really interesting. Some of those mutations change the proteins the cancer makes. Your cells constantly break proteins into tiny pieces and then display some of those pieces for your immune system to inspect. An antigen is basically a molecular target your immune system can recognize and respond to. So if a cancer mutation creates a new antigen that someone's healthy cells usually doesn't have, that's a neoantigen. Moderna uses an algorithm to select up to 34 promising neoantigens from that tumor. Then they put genetic instructions for those targets into messenger RNA and manufacture treatments specifically for that patient. The goal is to train T cells in the immune system to recognize those targets and attack the cancer cells carrying them. Then they combine it with Keytruda which helps release some molecular break that can stop T cells from attacking. Now about phase three. New drugs are tested in stages for a reason. Phase one mainly asks, can humans take this safely enough and what dose should we use? Phase two asks, does it actually show enough evidence of working to justify a bigger test? And phase three is the large controlled test. It's designed to confirm whether the benefits and risks actually hold up next to another treatment. We don't really know exactly how large that phase three benefit is yet. The numbers haven't all been released. Overall survival is still being followed and this treatment is not yet approved. But each phase has to generate enough evidence to justify going further and Moderna and Merck just tested this in 1137 people. This is the first positive phase three result for an individualized neoantigen therapy and for an mRNA based cancer treatment. That's the breakthrough using your individual biological data to design a treatment made for you.
